public_messages: [Sara Johansson]: The proposed development poses significant risks to the nesting habitat of three shorebird species and the integrity of the dune ecosystem, which serves as a critical buffer against coastal flooding. Clearing 40% of the dune habitat would degrade its protective function and undermine its resilience to projected sea level rise, increasing flood risk to the island and adjacent areas. Ecological surveys, if limited to a single season, may not fully represent the biodiversity supported by the site, weakening the basis for mitigation. The economic benefits, while notable, do not outweigh the long-term ecological and public safety costs. Under applicable planning standards and wetland protection codes, Option B—blocking development—is the more defensible choice.

[Samuel Kowalski]: The proposed development would cause significant ecological harm by clearing 40% of the dune ecosystem, jeopardizing nesting habitat for three shorebird species and reducing the dune system's ability to buffer coastal flooding. Single-season ecological surveys may underestimate the site’s biodiversity and ecological value, limiting the reliability of any mitigation measures. The projected high flood risk due to sea level rise further undermines the long-term viability and safety of the development. Under wetland protection codes, the habitat function and resilience of the site must be preserved, and mitigation proposals must demonstrate ecological equivalency—neither of which is convincingly demonstrated here. Given the cumulative risks and the lack of adequate mitigation, Option B—blocking development—aligns with the principles of habitat protection and public safety outlined in planning standards.
